Outlet: CBS News / AP, published November 7, 2026 / 9:20 AM EST (14:20 GMT)

# Zelenskyy accuses Russia of ramping up attacks on Ukraine ahead of U.S. talks
By CBS/AP

Missile attacks struck across Ukraine on Saturday, wounding at least nine people, as Kyiv and Moscow prepared for new talks next week with the United States.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Russia used 36 missiles to target critical infrastructure. Only four missiles were taken down, Zelenskyy said, highlighting a shortage of interceptors. He also said 172 drones were used in the attacks, which struck Kyiv and 12 other regions.

The president accused Russia of intensifying its attacks on Ukraine and the country's infrastructure ahead of trilateral talks.

Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war. The new round of negotiations would be the fourth brokered by the Trump administration, the most recent having been in Geneva in February.

Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the impasse while acknowledging that territorial and security questions remain unresolved.

"Russia has a very particular view of diplomacy" that differs significantly from Western approaches, Zelenskyy stated. He added: "We hope that the United States, like our other partners, will act on principle."

Russian attacks target Ukrainian infrastructure

The Russian missiles that hit overnight across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, damaged homes and commercial properties, triggering new power and water outages, national and city authorities said.

Zelenskyy said a kindergarten was "partially destroyed." Photos show rubble near the damaged building.

Kateryna Korniichuk, 64, was at home with her granddaughter when an attack hit. She told The Associated Press: "The first blast wave threw us against that wall and then against the other wall, because we were in the corridor. It's very hard. No sleep, no peace" and neither children nor adults could rest.

Strikes also prompted officials to close Kyiv's 892-yard-long Northern Bridge, a major route connecting the city with large residential areas on the east bank of the Dnipro River. Russia's Ministry of Defense confirmed Saturday that it had targeted the bridge, saying that it facilitated the transport of weaponry, military hardware and specialist equipment for Ukraine's armed forces.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that work was already underway to repair the city's Northern Bridge and that water pressure in Kyiv had been stabilized. Earlier Saturday, he had described the city's energy situation as "extremely difficult, affecting the city's heating and water supply systems."

Ukraine's Energy Ministry said Saturday's missile attacks damaged networks that carry electricity from nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central regions, as well as multiple other power facilities. It said outages were most widespread in the Kyiv and central Zhytomyr regions, as well as in the eastern regions of Kharkiv, Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk.

The outages were separate from scheduled rolling blackouts imposed to protect the grid, which remain in effect across much of Ukraine.

Russia also said that it had targeted an industrial facility in the capital producing Flamingo missiles, as well as a power station, an electrical substation, and a plant producing ammunition, explosives and gunpowder in the wider Kyiv region. It also confirmed striking an electrical substation in the Zhytomyr region.

Zelenskyy said that at one energy facility, preliminary findings show Russia used KN-23 missiles "manufactured and supplied by North Korea." He called the use of the alleged North Korean missile "further proof that global sanctions regimes need to be significantly strengthened." Technical assessments at other sites are ongoing.

Recovery efforts continue after massive attack

Meanwhile, in southern Ukraine, a recovery operation continued into its sixth day in the village of Komyshuvakha, devastated on Monday when multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter as residents waited for humanitarian aid.

Emergency services said they had recovered nine more bodies in the previous 24 hours, bringing the death toll early Saturday morning to 55. Dozens of people remain missing.

Village resident Mykola Krasnov, 72, said he was still looking for his wife but had heard no word from rescuers. He asked: "She went to get humanitarian aid, and a 3-ton bomb was dropped there. Where is she?" He added that she had not come home, that rescuers had not found her body, and she was not in the morgue or alive at the scene.

The village of Komyshuvakha is located near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region.

Russia reports drone strikes

A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia's Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said Saturday.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov Seas, it said.

The head of Russia's southwestern Saratov region, Gov. Roman Busargin, wrote on social media that a drone attack damaged "civilian infrastructure" and several residential buildings in the area. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.

The head of Russia's Oryol region, Gov. Andrey Klychkov, also said Saturday that a Ukrainian attack had damaged commercial warehouse and production sites in the regional capital, as cited by state media.

Russian media outlets reported that a Ukrainian attack sparked a blaze at Oryol's Proton-Electrotex plant, which produces components for military equipment.
